introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et mention manuscrite d'adresse web ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les effectifs sont donnés en ordres de grandeur prudents (« roughly nine to ten million », « about two million »).

Question 2 : l'énoncé imprimé associe « the Jihad in Futa Jallon » aux dates 1854-1864. Ces dates correspondent à la guerre sainte d'Al-Hajj Umar Tall (empire toucouleur, parti de Dinguiraye, en bordure du Fouta-Djalon), alors que le jihad du Fouta-Djalon proprement dit date d'environ 1725 (Karamoko Alfa). Le sujet est recopié tel quel ; le corrigé signale la divergence et traite le mouvement de 1854-1864, avec le jihad du Fouta-Djalon en arrière-plan. L'année de début de la guerre sainte d'Umar est donnée de façon prudente (1852 ou 1854 selon les sources).

Question 2 : détails à vérifier par un historien (siège de Médine en 1857, prise de Ségou en 1861 et de Hamdallahi en 1862, mort d'Umar en 1864, chute de Ségou face à Archinard en 1890) ; ils sont cités conformément à l'historiographie courante, mais le corrigé ne s'appuie pas sur des chiffres.

Question 7 : les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, invitation des « Immortal Seven » et acquittement des sept évêques le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre) ; le corrigé précise le choix du calendrier julien.
Question 4 : le massacre de Thiaroye (décembre 1944), les émeutes d'Accra (1948) et la conférence de Brazzaville (1944) sont cités sans bilan chiffré, le nombre exact de victimes étant discuté.

Question 5 : exemples de coups d'État (Togo 1963, Ghana 1966, Nigeria 1966, Ouganda 1971, Éthiopie 1974, Mali 2020) cités sans chiffres ; la formule « very many people were killed » remplace volontairement tout bilan sous Amin, très discuté.

Question 12 : la liste des suspensions et départs (Nigeria 1995, Fidji, Zimbabwe 2003, Gambie 2013 puis retour 2018) et l'adhésion du Cameroun en 1995 sont citées de mémoire historique ; aucun chiffre financier n'est avancé.

Questions à thème régional : les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `military coups in africa`, `refugee crisis in africa`, `league of nations`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à reverifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent was the abolition of slave trade in West Africa motivated by British self-interest?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Atlantic slave trade was made illegal for British subjects by the Slave Trade Act of 1807, and Britain then used diplomacy, the Royal Navy and colonial footholds to suppress the trade on the West African coast during the nineteenth century. The question asks whether this campaign was driven mainly by British self-interest (economic, strategic and political gain) or by genuine humanitarian and religious conviction. A balanced judgement is that humanitarianism started the movement, but self-interest decided its timing, its methods and its long-term consequences for West Africa.

**1. The case for humanitarian motives (the limits of the self-interest argument).**
- Abolition was pushed by a mass movement of Evangelicals, Quakers and reformers such as William Wilberforce, Thomas Clarkson, Granville Sharp and, later, Thomas Fowell Buxton. Petitions, boycotts of slave-grown sugar and publications such as Olaudah Equiano's autobiography (1789) created strong public opinion.
- Britain kept up the suppression at a financial cost: the West Africa Squadron, created in 1808, was expensive to maintain and lost many sailors to tropical disease. Africans freed from captured ships were landed at Freetown, Sierra Leone, where the colony had been founded in 1787 as a settlement for freed people.
- Missionary societies carried the moral argument into West Africa; the Niger Expedition of 1841, inspired by Buxton, aimed to replace the slave trade with Christianity, commerce and civilisation.

**2. The case for self-interest.**
- *Economic change at home.* The Industrial Revolution made Britain a manufacturing power in need of raw materials (palm oil for lubricants and soap, later groundnuts) and of wider markets for cotton and metal goods. "Legitimate commerce" in palm oil promised a more profitable and more stable relationship with West Africa than the slave trade did.
- *The declining value of the slave system.* Historians such as Eric Williams (*Capitalism and Slavery*, 1944) argued that the West Indian plantation economy was losing its importance and that abolition followed economic decline. Other historians, notably Seymour Drescher, have argued that the trade was still profitable when it was abolished, so the economic motive was not the only explanation; the debate is unresolved and should be presented as such.
- *Rivalry with other powers.* Ending the trade for British ships also hit British rivals; after 1807 Britain pressed France, Spain and Portugal to follow, and used the right to search ships to extend its naval control of the Atlantic. Suppression gave Britain a pretext for a permanent naval and commercial presence on the coast.
- *Strategic and territorial expansion.* Anti-slavery was used to justify intervention. In 1851 the Royal Navy bombarded Lagos to remove Oba Kosoko, a slave trader in British eyes, and to install Akitoye, who accepted a treaty banning the trade; Lagos was annexed in 1861. Treaties against the trade were signed with many coastal rulers, and consuls (such as John Beecroft, appointed for the Bights of Benin and Biafra in 1849) acquired growing influence. In the Cameroon coastal area, British missionaries (Joseph Merrick at Bimbia, Alfred Saker at Douala from the 1840s) and traders followed the same pattern of mission, treaty and commerce.
- *Security of trade.* Palm-oil traders wanted peaceful routes and stable coastal states, and slave-raiding states such as Dahomey were seen as obstacles to commerce.

**3. Evaluation.** The two motives were not opposed: for many British abolitionists, humanitarian and commercial arguments reinforced each other, and anti-slavery was also a popular cause that governments could adopt at low political cost. Humanitarian pressure explains why abolition was *started* in 1807 and why the suppression was maintained; self-interest explains why it was extended into West Africa through naval power, treaties and eventually colonial annexation, and why Britain chose legitimate commerce over any other form of relationship. The effects on Africa were also mixed: the export of captives declined, but internal slavery often grew, because slave labour was used to produce palm oil and other exports.

**Conclusion.** Abolition was not purely selfless, nor was it merely a mask for British economic interests. To a *large extent* the timing and methods of abolition in West Africa served British commercial, naval and strategic interests, but the movement could not have succeeded without a strong humanitarian conviction that made suppression politically possible.
